title: Hypnogram Builder
description: Interactive hypnogram of an illustrative 9-hour teen night with cycles of about 90 minutes. Clicking a stage label or hovering over the night shows a schematic EEG trace for Wake, N1, N2, N3, or REM, and a slider shortens the night to show how many minutes of REM, N2, and N3 are lost.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
learningObjectives: Identify each sleep stage (Wake, N1, N2, N3, REM) from its schematic EEG signature.
Describe how sleep stages are distributed across a night, with most N3 early and longer REM periods late.
Interpret a hypnogram to explain why cutting a 9-hour night to 6 hours removes about half of REM sleep but almost no N3 sleep.
prerequisites: Frequency and amplitude of brain waves (Chapter 10, Section 10.3)
Names of the four sleep stages (Chapter 10, Section 10.5)
keyQuestions: Which sleep stage has the tallest, slowest EEG waves?
Why do REM periods get longer toward morning?
Which stages are lost when a night of sleep is cut short at the end, and why?
misconceptions: Short sleep removes a little of every stage evenly. In fact, cutting the end of the night removes mostly REM and N2 sleep.
The brain shuts off during sleep. In fact, each stage has its own active EEG pattern, and REM looks much like waking.
Deep sleep happens evenly all night. In fact, most N3 occurs in the first half of the night.
accessibility: Screen-reader description via p5 describe(); stage menu provides keyboard access to all EEG traces; text 14px or larger.

controls.name: Hours of sleep
controls.purpose: Moves the alarm line to cut the night short

controls.name: Show EEG for
controls.purpose: Chooses which schematic EEG trace is shown

assumptions: The night is an illustrative composite for a healthy teen, not a real recording.
Cycles last about 90 minutes; N3 occurs in the first four cycles; REM periods grow from 10 to 35 minutes.
Shortening sleep removes time from the end of the night.
limitations: Real hypnograms vary from person to person and night to night.
EEG traces are schematic shapes; only their approximate frequencies and relative sizes are meaningful.
Going to bed later shifts circadian timing in ways this simple model does not show.
